title: In the woods
hookLine: Emerson: in the woods we return to reason and faith
carry: among trees, reason and faith come back together
last: WONDER IS OWED TO WHAT COMES EVERY NIGHT.

cards: Reason and faith. Put those two words side by side at a dinner table and you might start an argument, with someone casting them as rivals.
Emerson, in the first chapter of Nature, puts them in the same sentence, on the same path, among trees. He doesn't say the woods give you one or the other. He says you get both back.
And the word he uses is return, as though both were yours once, and you wandered off.

teach.h: IN THE WOODS, IS PERPETUAL YOUTH.
teach.b: First, the age you are in the woods. "In the woods, is perpetual youth." There, Emerson says, a person sheds their years the way a snake sheds its skin, and at any age is a child again.
Not childish. Fresh. Second, the line itself.
"In the woods, we return to reason and faith." Reason: the clear, unhurried mind that can see what's true. Faith: trust, a sense that the world holds together.
Emerson doesn't make them fight; both come back when the noise drops away. Third, the promise.
Among the trees, he says, he feels nothing can happen to him in life, no disgrace, no disaster, that nature can't repair, as long as he keeps his eyes.
That's a big claim, and it's his, from a man who had buried his young wife. He isn't saying nothing will hurt. He's saying the woods are a place where repair begins.
Fourth, where the paragraph goes next. Standing on bare ground, he writes, all mean egotism vanishes.
"I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all." That eye-ball had a day of its own, back on day one thousand twenty-two.

The self gets small, and the seeing gets large: among trees, you stop being the center of the picture. Far from any forest, that might be a single tree on a city street, a park at lunch, a row of bushes by a bus stop.

how: Readers of Emerson's Nature often take walks among trees as a quiet practice of their own, sometimes carrying this passage with them, to let reason and trust settle at the same time.

o: a place Emerson went to hide from his critics
Emerson's place where reason and faith both come back
a retreat where you leave reason behind for faith

games.q: inside in the woods: tap the pairs.
p: I am nothing; I see all

s: Emerson says the woods give you reason instead of faith
he says in the woods we return to reason and faith, both.
he says in the woods a person is a child again at any age
he compares it to a snake shedding its skin.
Emerson promises that nothing bad will happen in the woods
he says nothing can befall him that nature cannot repair, which is about repair, not escape.

games.q: Emerson is standing on bare ground among trees. what does he say happens to his ego?
o: nothing; he just enjoys the view.
games.why: all mean egotism vanishes, and he becomes a transparent eye-ball: "I am nothing; I see all."

practice: If you can, go outside and walk slowly toward the nearest tree; if you can't, bring to mind the last time you stood among trees, the smell, the light through leaves, the sound underfoot.
Either way, let your mind get quiet enough to notice two things, something clear and something steady, without needing to name them reason and faith.

carryVoice: Your line: among trees, reason and faith come back together. Emerson's word is return, as if you'd been there before. Go gently.
